groups.title: Advanced Caching Theory
groups.question: Three server components on one page fetch the same user, a page shows stale posts after an edit, and you want to refresh only post-related data. Explain how Next.js caching works at this level.

followUps.Request memoization within a single rend: Why don't three identical fetches in one render cause three requests?
followUps.Data Cache vs Full Route Cache differenc: What is the difference between the Data Cache and the Full Route Cache?
followUps.Tag-based cache invalidation for fine co: How do cache tags let you refresh just post data?

evidence.text: Identical fetch calls during one server render are deduplicated.
This only lasts for that single render.
Each component can fetch what it needs without passing data down.
The Data Cache stores fetch results between requests.
The Full Route Cache stores the rendered HTML of static routes.
Knowing which one is stale tells you what to revalidate.
fetch calls can be tagged, such as with posts.
revalidateTag clears only entries with that tag.
This avoids clearing unrelated cached data.

groups.title: Runtime Considerations
groups.question: One route must use a Node library that reads files, another should run close to users worldwide, and a stock price page must never be cached. Explain the runtime and caching choices.

followUps.Edge runtime vs Node.js runtime trade-of: When would you choose the edge runtime over Node.js?
followUps.Avoiding stale data with cache: no-store: What does cache no-store do and when do you need it?

evidence.text: The edge runtime starts quickly and runs close to users.
It lacks many Node.js APIs, like the file system.
Routes needing Node libraries use the Node runtime; light, latency-sensitive ones can use the edge.
no-store skips the Data Cache for that fetch.
Every request fetches fresh data.
It suits data that must always be current, like prices or account balances.

groups.title: Client-Side Data Management
groups.question: A client-side dashboard widget needs live data, optimistic updates and a second query that depends on the first. Explain how you would use TanStack Query.

followUps.TanStack Query for client-side server st: Why use TanStack Query in client components alongside server components?
followUps.Optimistic updates with useMutation: How does useMutation support optimistic updates?
followUps.Parallel and dependent queries with useQ: How do you make one query wait for another?

evidence.text: It manages server data in client components.
It handles background refetching, stale time and invalidation.
Server components cover initial data; TanStack Query covers interactive, live client data.
onMutate applies the expected change to the cache before the request.
onError rolls back to the saved previous value.
onSettled refetches to sync with the server.

notEnough: Only saying it updates the UI early.

evidence.text: Several useQuery calls run in parallel by default.
The enabled option holds a query until its input is ready.
For example, a user's projects query waits until the user id is known.

notEnough: Only saying queries can depend on each other.

groups.title: ISR and On-demand Revalidation
groups.question: Your blog pages are static, but editors want new posts live within a minute or instantly after publishing. Explain how ISR and on-demand revalidation work.

followUps.Incremental Static Regeneration with rev: What does exporting revalidate = 60 from a page do?
followUps.On-demand revalidation via webhook route: How would a CMS webhook refresh pages instantly?

evidence.text: The page is regenerated at most every 60 seconds.
Visitors get the cached page while a new one is built in the background.
This gives static speed with near-real-time freshness.
A route handler receives the CMS webhook.
It checks a secret so only the CMS can trigger it.
It calls revalidatePath or revalidateTag to refresh the affected pages without redeploying.

notEnough: Only saying the webhook triggers revalidation.
